title: Process Scheduling
misconceptions: A process always uses the CPU continuously until it completes its execution.
First-Come First-Served scheduling guarantees the fastest average response time.
Preemptive scheduling allows processes to run to completion without interruption.
Priority scheduling completely prevents process starvation.

rubric.text: Defines process scheduling as allocating CPU execution time to processes in the ready queue.
Defines non-preemptive scheduling as allowing a process to retain the CPU until voluntary release.
Defines preemptive scheduling as allowing the operating system to interrupt a running process.
Explains that process execution consists of alternating CPU bursts separated by I/O waits.
Describes First-Come First-Served scheduling as running processes purely in arrival order.
States that First-Come First-Served scheduling can cause a convoy effect that worsens average wait time.
Explains Shortest Job First scheduling as selecting the process with the smallest upcoming CPU burst.
Defines starvation as indefinite waiting experienced by low priority processes.
Explains aging as a mechanism of increasing process priority over time to prevent starvation.
